sections.title: 1. Purpose and place in the outline

blocks.text: The outline gives Fine Arts two halves (§3H):
Music: folk songs, hymns, rhythm and pitch, and composer study, one composer per term, aligned to the history period.
Art: picture study, one artist per term, drawing fundamentals, and hands-on work in the medium of the period studied.

For Grade 3, the Colonial year, the outline names Baroque and Classical composers and colonial folk art and portraiture (§4). So this year the child listens to six composers from Vivaldi to Beethoven, studies six American artists of the period from John White to Edward Hicks, learns to draw, and makes the things colonial people made: silhouettes, samplers, stencils, watercolors.

Like the rest of the grammar stage, Fine Arts is about looking and listening closely and coming to know a few great things well, not art theory. The child learns the names, the works and the stories, and keeps their own work in the portfolio.

blocks.text: Why these. The composers run in order from early Baroque to the edge of the Romantic era, so the child hears music change over the same years History covers. The artists are American painters of the period, and their subjects are the year's history: John White painted the Roanoke voyage (History Term 1), Copley painted Paul Revere, Peale and Stuart painted Washington, Audubon traveled the frontier, and Hicks was a Quaker folk painter of William Penn's Pennsylvania.
The traditional method, about 15 minutes:
1. Look at the painting quietly for two or three minutes. Notice everything.
2. Turn it over and narrate: what was in it, where, what colors, what was happening.
3. Look again and see what was missed.
4. Tell the child the painting's title and artist, and one or two facts about it.

Six paintings per artist, one a week; the term manual names them. All are old enough to be in the public domain, and good reproductions are free from museum open-access collections, such as the National Gallery of Art and the Metropolitan Museum. Print them, or show them on a screen.
One piece a week, heard two or three times across the week: once just listening, once while drawing or moving to it, once to narrate ("What did it make you think of?").
A short story from the composer's life each week, told by the parent.
By ear: by the end of the term, the child can name the composer of the term's best-known piece when they hear it.
Recordings are easy to find free online, through public-library music services, or on inexpensive CDs. The term manual names each piece.
Folk songs: one or two a term from the period (§3), sung until known.

Hymns: the Bible course's hymn of the term (Doxology, "All People…", "Joy to the World", "A Mighty Fortress", "O God, Our Help", "Amazing Grace") is sung here too. Fine Arts doesn't add hymns of its own.
Rhythm: a steady beat; clapping rhythms; the note values whole, half, quarter and eighth.
Pitch: high and low; the first notes of the scale, do, re, mi, fa, sol, sung and shown with hand signs.

The quadrivium link (§1): music is "number in time". In Term 5, when Arithmetic teaches fractions, note values are the same idea: a half note lasts half as long as a whole note, and two quarters make a half. The Term 5 manual makes the connection explicit.
Instrument lessons (recorder, piano, violin) are an elective (§6), not part of this course.
Through the year, the drawing lessons (task C, on weeks without a project) build these skills:
Line and shape: drawing what you see as simple shapes.
Observation: drawing from life, slowly; the nature journal (Science) is the daily practice ground.
Shading: light and dark, with pencil pressure.
Proportion: the proportions of a face (Term 4, with the portraits).
Simple perspective: near things big, far things small; the horizon line.
Still life and nature: fruit, leaves, birds (Term 5, with Audubon).
Fine Arts isn't graded.
Narration of each painting and each piece: oral, every week.
Portfolio: the term's best drawing and its hands-on project go into the portfolio (§8).

Term-end check (week 6, oral, about 10 minutes): the child names the term's artist and composer; describes a favorite painting; names the composer of two or three pieces by ear; sings the folk song. Not scored; it's a conversation.
Memory Work (11) gets a card each term: the composer and the artist, with their dates.

head: Course
Link
rows: The artists painted the year's history; the composers lived through it
The hymns are sung in both courses; Handel's Messiah sets Bible texts
The nature journal is drawing practice; natural dyes (Science Term 5) give colors for painting
Composer and artist cards each term

blocks.text: Fine Arts carries over freely (§7). A missed week moves the sequence later; nothing is lost.
Composer listening is easy to keep going in a busy week: play the piece at a meal or in the car.
Projects can spread over two weeks if they take longer.

Colored pencils and a good drawing pencil, a sketchbook, a child's watercolor set and brushes, black and white paper, scissors and glue, cross-stitch fabric and thread with a blunt needle, stencil card or a manila folder, and a way to play recordings. Each term manual lists anything special.

For each term: where to find the paintings and recordings, the folk song words, and the term-end conversation questions.

head: Composer
Antonio Vivaldi (1678–1741): The Four Seasons
rows: John White (about 1539–1593): watercolors of the Roanoke voyage
Line and shape · drawing from life · light and dark
"Over the River and Through the Wood" · the Doxology (Bible's hymn)
Steady beat · fast and slow · loud and soft · quarter and eighth notes

glance.text: The tasks each week: A, picture study · B, composer study · C, drawing or watercolor · D, singing and rhythm. Any order.

reference.title: Where to find the paintings and music

blocks.text: John White's watercolors are in the British Museum, London, and are widely reproduced. Search the museum's online collection or any search engine for "John White" with the painting's subject. Titles vary a little between collections; the subject is what matters. The originals are over 400 years old and in the public domain.
Vivaldi's The Four Seasons and his Gloria are among the most recorded pieces in the world: free online, through a public library, or on any inexpensive recording.

John White sailed with the English voyages to Roanoke Island in the 1580s, and in 1587 became governor of the colony that History reads about in week 2, the "Lost Colony". He painted the people of the coast, their towns, and the animals and plants he saw, so that people in England could see the New World. They're among the first pictures of North America painted by an English artist.

Antonio Vivaldi lived in Venice, Italy. He was a priest, and because of his red hair he was called "the Red Priest". For many years he taught music at an orphanage for girls, the Ospedale della Pietà, whose orchestra became famous. He wrote about 500 concertos. The Four Seasons (published 1725) is four violin concertos, one for each season, each with a short poem describing what the music shows.
The town of Secotan. A village of houses, fields of corn and people at work and at worship. Look, turn over, narrate, look again.
Spring, first movement (Allegro). Listen for birds singing (the violins trill), a brook, and a thunderstorm in the middle. Story: Vivaldi, the Red Priest of Venice.
Line and shape. Everything can be drawn as simple shapes. Draw a cup, a chair and a tree, starting each with circles, rectangles and triangles, then adding lines.
Learn "Over the River", the first stanza. Steady beat: pat your knees in time with the song.
Indians fishing. Men in a canoe, fish traps, and fish in the water. (History reads about Roanoke this week.)
Summer, third movement (Presto): a summer storm, fast and wild. Story: the Ospedale della Pietà and its orchestra of girls.
Washes. Wet a sheet of watercolor paper lightly; brush on one color and watch it spread. Then try a wash that fades from dark to light. White painted his skies and water this way.
"Over the River", both stanzas. Fast and slow: clap along with Summer's storm (fast), then Spring's opening (slower).
The town of Pomeiooc. A round village with a wall of posts around it. Compare it with Secotan from week 1.
Autumn, first movement (Allegro): a harvest dance and a celebration. (It fits the season, and the Pilgrims' harvest in History and Literature.)
Drawing from life. Bring in a leaf. Draw it slowly, looking more at the leaf than the paper: its outline, then its veins. Science link: this is the same skill as the nature journal.
"Over the River" and the Doxology. Loud and soft: sing a stanza softly, then loudly; listen for loud and soft in Autumn.
A loggerhead turtle. One of White's paintings of animals. Notice how carefully he painted the shell's pattern.
Winter, second movement (Largo): sitting warm by the fire while rain falls outside. The plucked strings are the raindrops.
Paint an animal like White. Draw a turtle or fish lightly in pencil, paint a pale wash over it, let it dry, then add darker details with a small brush.
Quarter notes, said "ta": clap four steady tas. Clap the rhythm of "O-ver the ri-ver".
A flying fish. White painted the creatures he saw on the voyage across the ocean. Why might people in England have wanted to see a fish that could fly?
Winter, first movement (Allegro non molto): shivering in the icy wind, stamping feet, teeth chattering.
Light and dark. Draw a circle. Shade one side dark and let it fade to light on the other side: now it looks like a ball. Then shade an apple the same way.
Eighth notes, said "ti-ti": two quick notes in one beat. Clap ta, ta, ti-ti, ta.

intro.text: Term-end conversation (week 6)
A friendly conversation, not a test:
1. Who painted this term's pictures? What did he paint, and why?
2. Which painting is your favorite? Describe it without looking.
3. Listen to three short clips (Spring, Summer, Winter): which season is each?
4. Who wrote The Four Seasons? What was he called, and why?
5. Sing "Over the River and Through the Wood".
Memory Work card: Vivaldi (1678–1741), The Four Seasons · John White (about 1539–1593), watercolors of Roanoke

blocks.text: Dancers around a circle of posts. People dancing in a ring at a festival. Then lay out all six pictures and choose a favorite.
Vivaldi's Gloria, the opening chorus "Gloria in excelsis Deo" ("Glory to God in the highest"). It's the angels' song from Luke 2, which Bible memorizes in Term 3.
Finish a watercolor for the portfolio: a village scene, an animal or a fish, in the way White painted.
Sing "Over the River" and the Doxology for the family.

after.title: "Over the River and Through the Wood"

blocks.text: Words by Lydia Maria Child, 1844 (public domain). The first two stanzas.
Over the river, and through the wood,
To Grandfather's house we go;
The horse knows the way
To carry the sleigh
Through the white and drifted snow.
Over the river, and through the wood—
Oh, how the wind does blow!
It stings the toes
And bites the nose,
As over the ground we go.
Picture study is quiet looking. Resist explaining the painting first. Let the child find what's there; add a fact or two afterward.
Play the music in the background at other times in the week, too: at meals, in the car. Familiarity is the whole point.
Watercolor is forgiving. Let the paper dry between layers, and expect blotches. White's own paintings have them.

Watercolor paper or heavy drawing paper · a child's watercolor set · two brushes (one large, one small) · a drawing pencil · a sketchbook · a leaf · an apple · printed or on-screen copies of the six paintings · recordings of The Four Seasons and the Gloria

head: Composer
Johann Sebastian Bach (1685–1750)
rows: John Singleton Copley (1738–1815): portraits of colonial Boston
A cross-stitch sampler, as colonial children made
"Simple Gifts" (1848) · "All People That on Earth Do Dwell" (Bible's hymn)
Half and whole notes · rests · marches and waltzes

reference.title: Where to find the paintings and music

blocks.text: Copley's paintings are in American museums, chiefly the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, and the National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C. Both have free online images. All are in the public domain.
Bach's music is among the most recorded in the world: free online, through a public library, or on any inexpensive recording.

John Singleton Copley grew up in Boston and taught himself to paint. By his twenties he was the finest portrait painter in the colonies, painting merchants, ministers and craftsmen, including Paul Revere, the silversmith Literature and History meet next term. In 1774, just before the Revolution, he moved to London and never returned.

Johann Sebastian Bach was born in Eisenach, Germany, in 1685, into a family of musicians. He was an organist, a choir director and a teacher, and he had twenty children. For his last 27 years he led the music at St. Thomas Church in Leipzig, writing new music for services almost every week. At the end of many of his pieces he wrote the letters S.D.G., for Soli Deo Gloria: "to God alone be the glory".
Epes Sargent (about 1760). An old merchant leaning on a stone pillar. Look closely at his hands and face.
"Jesu, Joy of Man's Desiring", from Cantata 147. Listen for the gentle flowing melody and the choir's hymn tune above it. Story: Bach's musical family.
Contour drawing. Put one hand on the table and draw its outline slowly with the other, looking at the hand almost the whole time. It will look odd; that's the point. You're training your eyes.
Learn "Simple Gifts", the first two lines. Half notes: one note held for two beats ("ta-a").
Boy with a Flying Squirrel (1765). Copley's half-brother Henry, with a pet flying squirrel on a chain. Copley sent it to London, where it made him famous.
Brandenburg Concerto No. 3, first movement. Listen to the strings chasing each other.

Plan the sampler. Colonial girls and boys stitched samplers to practice their letters and stitches. On graph paper, plan an alphabet (capitals A–Z, or just the child's initials), the child's name and the year, with a simple border. Penmanship is reviewing capitals this term too.
"Simple Gifts", the first verse. Whole notes: held for four beats ("ta-a-a-a").
Paul Revere (1768). Revere at his workbench with a silver teapot and his engraving tools. (Literature and History meet Revere in Term 3.)
Toccata and Fugue in D minor, for organ. Big, dramatic and famous. Talk about the organ: pipes, many keyboards, and pedals played with the feet.
Learn the stitches on a scrap of cross-stitch fabric: a running stitch for the border, then the cross-stitch (one slanted stitch, then another crossing it). Then start the first letters.
Rests: beats of silence. Clap ta, ta, rest, ta; the rest is a silent beat.
Samuel Adams (about 1772). Adams stands pointing to a document. What do you think he's saying?
"Air" from Orchestral Suite No. 3, often called "Air on the G String": slow and calm.

Still life. Set three objects on the table (a cup, an apple and a spoon) and draw them as they sit, with their shapes and shadows. Copley painted objects as carefully as faces: the squirrel's chain, Revere's teapot.
Marches and waltzes. March to a piece in fours (one-two-three-four); then sway to a waltz in threes (one-two-three). Which is "Simple Gifts"?
The Copley Family (1776–77). Copley painted his own family in London, with his children climbing over their grandfather and mother.
Cello Suite No. 1, Prelude. One cello playing alone, rolling like waves.
Keep stitching: the letters, then the child's name and the year.
Clap the rhythm of "Simple Gifts" while singing it.

intro.text: Term-end conversation (week 12)
1. Who painted this term's portraits? Where did he live, and where did he move?
2. Which portrait is your favorite? Describe it without looking.
3. Listen to three clips ("Jesu, Joy", the Toccata, the Air): can you tell they're all by the same composer? What are they played on?
4. What did Bach write at the end of his music, and what does it mean?
5. Sing "Simple Gifts".
Memory Work card: Bach (1685–1750), "S.D.G.: to God alone be the glory" · John Singleton Copley (1738–1815), portraits of colonial Boston

blocks.text: Watson and the Shark (1778). A dramatic rescue in Havana harbor: sailors in a boat pull a boy out of the water as a shark comes near. Then lay out all six paintings and choose a favorite.
"Sheep May Safely Graze", from Cantata 208. Gentle music about a good shepherd. (It suits Psalm 22 [23] from Bible Term 1.)
Finish the border and mount the sampler on card or in a simple frame for the portfolio. If it isn't finished, it can carry into Term 3.
Sing "Simple Gifts" and "All People That on Earth Do Dwell" for the family.
Words and tune by Joseph Brackett, a Shaker of Maine, 1848 (public domain).
'Tis the gift to be simple, 'tis the gift to be free,
'Tis the gift to come down where we ought to be,
And when we find ourselves in the place just right,
'Twill be in the valley of love and delight.
When true simplicity is gained,
To bow and to bend we shan't be ashamed,
To turn, turn will be our delight,
Till by turning, turning we come round right.
Samplers take patience. A simple sampler, such as initials, the year and a border, is plenty for a first one. The Hearth track's sewing (§6) can count it too.
Use a blunt tapestry needle and fabric with large, easy-to-see holes (Aida cloth).
Bach is everywhere. Children often find they already know a Bach tune from a film or an advertisement. Let them notice it.

Graph paper · cross-stitch (Aida) fabric, embroidery thread and a blunt tapestry needle · an embroidery hoop (optional) · drawing pencil and sketchbook · a cup, an apple and a spoon · printed or on-screen copies of the six paintings · Bach recordings

head: Composer
George Frideric Handel (1685–1759): Messiah, in the Christmas term
rows: Charles Willson Peale (1741–1827): portraits of the Revolution
Cut-paper silhouettes, a favorite way to make a likeness in the 1700s and 1800s
Profiles · simple perspective · animals from shapes
"Yankee Doodle" · "Chester" by William Billings · "Joy to the World" (Bible's hymn)
High and low · do, re, mi, fa, sol with hand signs

reference.title: Where to find the paintings and music

blocks.text: Peale's paintings are in American museums, chiefly the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts and the Philadelphia Museum of Art, with others at Washington and Lee University and the New-York Historical Society. Free online images are easy to find. All are in the public domain.
Handel's music, especially Messiah, is widely recorded, and many churches and towns perform Messiah at Christmas. If there's a performance nearby, go.

Charles Willson Peale was a saddle-maker from Maryland who became a painter. He fought in the Revolution and painted George Washington from life several times, beginning in 1772, the first portrait ever made of him. After the war he opened one of America's first museums in Philadelphia, full of portraits, stuffed animals and fossils. He named many of his children after painters: Raphaelle, Rembrandt, Rubens and Titian.

George Frideric Handel was born in Halle, Germany, in 1685, the same year as Bach. He moved to London and became the most famous composer in England. In 1741 he wrote Messiah, a long work for choir, soloists and orchestra that tells the Christian story using words from the Bible, in about three weeks. It was first performed in Dublin in 1742, and has been sung every year since.
The Peale Family (about 1771–73). Peale painted himself at work, surrounded by his family.
Messiah: "For unto us a child is born", words from Isaiah. Listen for the voices taking turns and then joining together. Story: Handel and Bach, born the same year.
Profiles. Have someone sit sideways to you. Draw the line of their face in profile: forehead, nose, lips, chin. It's the shape a silhouette is made from.
Learn "Yankee Doodle", the first verse and chorus. High and low: the parent sings a high note and a low note; the child shows high with hands up and low with hands down.
George Washington (1772). The first portrait of Washington, painted at Mount Vernon in the uniform of the Virginia militia, before the Revolution.
Messiah: "Glory to God", the angels' song to the shepherds, from Luke 2, the passage Bible is memorizing this term.

Trace a shadow. In a dark room, seat a family member sideways between a lamp and a sheet of paper taped to the wall. Trace the shadow of their profile. Cut it out, lay it on black paper, trace and cut again, and mount the black silhouette on white card.
Do, mi, sol with hand signs: do a fist at the waist, mi a flat hand at the chest, sol an open hand at the chin. Sing them up and down.
George Washington at Princeton (1779). Washington after his victories at Trenton and Princeton, with captured flags at his feet. (History reads about Trenton this term.)
Messiah: "Hallelujah" chorus. By tradition, audiences stand during it. Ask: why would people want to stand?
Simple perspective. Draw a road going away to the horizon: two lines that come together at a point. Add trees that get smaller as they get farther away.
Do, re, mi: add re (hand slanting up at the waist). Sing do re mi, mi re do.
The Staircase Group (1795). Two of Peale's sons on a staircase, painted so real that, the story goes, George Washington once bowed to them as he walked past.
Water Music: Hornpipe. Handel wrote Water Music in 1717 to be played on a barge floating on the River Thames for King George I.
Cut a silhouette of an animal or object: a horse, a ship, a tree, a tri-cornered hat. Draw the outline on the back of black paper, cut it out, and mount it.

Learn "Chester" by William Billings, the first verse. Billings was a Boston tanner who became one of America's first composers; "Chester" was sung by soldiers in the Revolution. Then sing do re mi fa sol (add fa, a thumb pointing down, and sol).
Exhumation of the Mastodon (1806–08). Peale painted his own dig for the bones of a huge, long-extinct animal in New York. He later showed the skeleton in his museum.
"The Arrival of the Queen of Sheba", from Solomon (1749). Bright, bustling music for the queen's visit to King Solomon. (Bible reads about Solomon this week.)
Animals from shapes. Draw a large animal, such as a mastodon, an elephant or a horse, starting with ovals for the body and head and rectangles for the legs. Then smooth the outline.
Sing "Yankee Doodle" and "Chester"; then "Joy to the World" (Bible's hymn).

intro.text: Term-end conversation (week 18)
1. Who painted this term's pictures? Why is his first portrait of Washington special?
2. Which painting is your favorite? Describe it without looking.
3. Listen to three clips ("Hallelujah", the Hornpipe, the Queen of Sheba): who wrote them?
4. What is Messiah, and where was it first performed?
5. Sing "Yankee Doodle" or "Chester", and show do, re, mi, fa, sol with hand signs.
Memory Work card: Handel (1685–1759), Messiah (1741) · Charles Willson Peale (1741–1827), the first portrait of Washington (1772)

blocks.text: The Artist in His Museum (1822). Peale, at 81, lifts a curtain to show his museum: portraits on the walls, birds in cases, and the mastodon. Then lay out all six paintings and choose a favorite.
Music for the Royal Fireworks (1749): La Réjouissance ("Rejoicing"), written for a celebration with fireworks in London.
Mount the term's silhouettes as a small gallery on one sheet: the family profile, the animal or object, and one more if there's time. The best goes in the portfolio.
Sing "Yankee Doodle", "Chester" and "Joy to the World" for the family.
Traditional, sung in the Revolution (public domain). One verse and the chorus.
Yankee Doodle went to town
A-riding on a pony,
Stuck a feather in his cap
And called it macaroni.
Yankee Doodle, keep it up,
Yankee Doodle dandy,
Mind the music and the step,
And with the girls be handy.
Words and music by William Billings, 1770 (public domain). The first verse.
Let tyrants shake their iron rod,
And Slav'ry clank her galling chains,
We fear them not, we trust in God,
New England's God for ever reigns.
Words to explain: tyrants (cruel rulers) · galling (rubbing, painful) · reigns (rules as king). The colonists sang that they wouldn't be ruled unjustly by Britain, because they trusted in God.
Messiah at Christmas. If a church or concert hall nearby performs it, going together is the best possible picture study and composer study in one.
Silhouettes need a dark room and a bright lamp. An older child can trace a younger sibling, and the other way round.
"Macaroni" in "Yankee Doodle" meant a fancy, fashionable style in the 1700s, not the pasta. Children enjoy knowing that.

Black and white paper · scissors and glue · a bright lamp and tape · drawing pencil and sketchbook · printed or on-screen copies of the six paintings · Handel recordings (Messiah, Water Music, Solomon, Royal Fireworks)

head: Composer
Joseph Haydn (1732–1809), "the father of the symphony"
rows: Gilbert Stuart (1755–1828): the portraits of George Washington
The proportions of a face · self-portrait · a portrait from life
"My Country, 'Tis of Thee" (1831) · "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God" (Bible's hymn)
The whole scale · steps and skips · the staff

reference.title: Where to find the paintings and music

blocks.text: Stuart's portraits are in the National Gallery of Art and the National Portrait Gallery, Washington, D.C., and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston. All have free online images, and all are in the public domain. The child already carries one Stuart in their pocket: his Washington is on the one-dollar bill.
Haydn's music is widely recorded: free online, through a public library, or on any inexpensive recording.

Gilbert Stuart was born in Rhode Island in 1755 and studied painting in London. When he came home in the 1790s he set out to paint George Washington, and did so several times. He painted the first six presidents. His unfinished "Athenaeum" portrait of Washington became the most famous picture of him in the world. In 1814, when British troops burned Washington, D.C., Dolley Madison had a full-length portrait of Washington in Stuart's style saved from the White House. (History tells of 1814 in Term 5.)

Joseph Haydn was born in a village in Austria in 1732, the son of a wheelwright. For about thirty years he was the music director for the Esterházy princes, writing for their orchestra almost every week. He wrote more than a hundred symphonies, which is why he is called "the father of the symphony". His musicians called him "Papa Haydn". He was a friend of Mozart (next term) and a teacher of the young Beethoven (Term 6).
The Skater (1782). A young man skating on a frozen lake in London. The painting made Stuart famous.
Symphony No. 94, "Surprise", second movement. Soft, gentle music, and then a sudden loud chord. The story goes that Haydn added it to wake up anyone who'd dozed off. Listen for it!

The proportions of a face. Draw an egg shape. The eyes go halfway down, not near the top. The nose is halfway between the eyes and the chin, and the mouth halfway between the nose and the chin. Draw a face on these guide lines.
Learn "My Country, 'Tis of Thee", the first verse. The whole scale: add la and ti and the high do to Term 3's do, re, mi, fa, sol. Sing up and down.
George Washington, the "Vaughan" portrait (1795). Stuart's first portrait of Washington from life.

Symphony No. 45, "Farewell", the end of the last movement. The prince kept his musicians away from their families too long, so Haydn wrote an ending in which the players stop and leave one by one, until only two violins are left. The prince took the hint.

Letter with a quill or dip pen. A goose feather cut to a point, or an inexpensive dip pen, and a bottle of ink. Practice strokes, then letters, slowly. Dip often; blot on scrap paper. (Penmanship's Term 4 lettering helps.)
Steps and skips: a step goes to the next note (do-re); a skip jumps over one (do-mi). Sing a few of each; the child says which.
George Washington, the "Lansdowne" portrait (1796). Washington standing, full-length, as president, with one arm held out.
String Quartet Op. 76 No. 3, "Emperor", second movement. Haydn wrote this hymn tune for the Austrian emperor, then wrote four variations on it for string quartet.
Self-portrait. Sit before a mirror and draw your own face, using the week 19 guide lines. Look often; draw slowly.
The staff: five lines and four spaces. Notes higher on the staff sound higher. Draw a staff and place do, re, mi on it.
George Washington, the "Athenaeum" portrait (1796). Stuart never finished it, and kept it to make copies from. Compare it with the one-dollar bill.
Trumpet Concerto, third movement. Bright, quick music for a new kind of trumpet with keys.
Letter a line from the Preamble: We the People of the United States, in quill or dip pen on good paper. (Literature recites the Preamble this term.)
Place notes on the staff as quarter, half and whole notes; sing what you've written.
Martha Washington (1796). The companion to the Athenaeum portrait, also left unfinished.
Symphony No. 101, "The Clock", second movement. Listen for the ticking of a clock in the strings and bassoons.
A portrait from life. Draw a family member, sitting still, using the guide lines. Stuart talked to his sitters to keep them lively. Try it.
Sing "My Country, 'Tis of Thee" and "A Mighty Fortress".

intro.text: Term-end conversation (week 24)
1. Who painted this term's portraits? Which of his portraits is on the one-dollar bill?
2. Which portrait is your favorite? Describe it without looking.
3. Listen to three clips (the "Surprise", "The Clock", the "Emperor" hymn): who wrote them? What's the story behind the "Surprise" or the "Farewell"?
4. Why is Haydn called "the father of the symphony"?
5. Sing "My Country, 'Tis of Thee".
Memory Work card: Haydn (1732–1809), "the father of the symphony" · Gilbert Stuart (1755–1828), the portraits of Washington

blocks.text: Thomas Jefferson (1805). Stuart's portrait of the third president. Then lay out all six portraits and choose a favorite.
The Creation: "The Heavens Are Telling", from Haydn's great choral work about the six days of Creation. The words come from Psalm 19. (Bible read Creation in Term 1.)
Finish the week 23 portrait for the portfolio, and mount the Preamble lettering beside it.
Sing "My Country, 'Tis of Thee" for the family.
Words by Samuel Francis Smith, 1831 (public domain). The first verse.
My country, 'tis of thee,
Sweet land of liberty,
Of thee I sing;
Land where my fathers died,
Land of the pilgrims' pride,
From ev'ry mountainside
Let freedom ring!
Point out the "pilgrims" from Term 1.
Faces are hard, and that's fine. The guide lines help more than talent does. Praise careful looking, not likeness.
Ink spills. Use a heavy jar or an ink bottle in a dish, old clothes, and newspaper on the table.
Listen for the stories. Haydn's music is full of jokes and surprises. Children love being in on them.

head: Composer
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (1756–1791)
rows: John James Audubon (1785–1851): The Birds of America
A bird drawn and painted in watercolor, as Audubon did
Birds from shapes · drawing from life · feathers and texture
"Shenandoah" · "The Star-Spangled Banner" · "O God, Our Help in Ages Past" (Bible's hymn)
Note values as fractions, alongside Arithmetic's fractions

reference.title: Where to find the paintings and music

blocks.text: Audubon's Birds of America prints are widely reproduced. The National Gallery of Art and many libraries and museums have free online images of the plates, and the National Audubon Society offers the whole set online. All are in the public domain.
Mozart's music is widely recorded: free online, through a public library, or on any inexpensive recording.

John James Audubon was born in 1785 on the island of Saint-Domingue (today's Haiti), grew up in France, and came to America as a young man. He traveled the frontier, through Kentucky, Ohio and down the Mississippi, watching and drawing birds. He painted every bird life-size, so the biggest birds had to be bent to fit the enormous pages. The Birds of America (1827–1838) has 435 plates; the book is so large it's called the "double elephant" size. (History follows the westward settlers this term; the nature journal follows the spring birds.)

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born in Salzburg, Austria, in 1756. He wrote his first pieces at five, and at six he was touring Europe with his father and sister, playing for kings and queens. He could play with a cloth over the keys. He wrote more than 600 works (symphonies, operas, concertos, church music) before he died in 1791, at only thirty-five. He was a friend of Haydn, last term's composer.

reference.title: Music as number: note values are fractions

blocks.text: This term Arithmetic teaches fractions. Music uses the same idea (outline §1: music is "number in time"):
Two halves make a whole; four quarters make a whole; two eighths make a quarter. Task D each week works through it.
Wild Turkey (Plate 1, the first plate in the book). A big male turkey striding through the grass.
Eine kleine Nachtmusik ("A Little Night Music"), first movement. Bright and well known. Story: Mozart the child performer.
Birds from shapes. Draw a bird as an oval body, a circle head and a triangle beak; then add the tail, wings and legs, and smooth the outline.
Learn "Shenandoah", the first verse. Note values as fractions: with Arithmetic's week 25 lesson, show that a half note is half of a whole note, and a quarter is a quarter of it.
Blue Jay. Three blue jays on a branch. Look at how Audubon shows them moving.
Twelve Variations on "Ah vous dirai-je, Maman". The tune is the one we sing as "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star". Mozart dresses it up twelve different ways. How many can you recognize?
Draw a real bird from life, in the yard or at a feeder: quickly, while it stays, then finish from memory. (The nature journal is watching spring birds too.)
Making a whole: how many quarters make a whole note? How many eighths make a half? Clap four quarters, then eight eighths, in the same time.
Carolina Parakeet. A flock of green, yellow and orange parakeets. This bird lived in the eastern United States in Audubon's day; it no longer exists.
The Magic Flute: "Der Vogelfänger bin ich ja" ("I am the bird-catcher"), sung by Papageno, a bird-catcher dressed in feathers. (It suits Audubon!)
Begin a bird painting. Choose a bird (from Audubon or from life) and draw it lightly in pencil, life-size if it fits, on a branch. Paint a pale first wash.

Filling a measure: a measure in 4/4 holds 4 beats. Write measures using different notes (a half and two quarters; four quarters; a whole) and clap them. Each measure must add up to 4, like an addition problem.
Snowy Owl. Two white owls at night. How does Audubon make white feathers show up?
Symphony No. 40, first movement. Restless and urgent. Compare it with the bright Eine kleine Nachtmusik.
Feathers and texture. Look closely at a real feather (or Audubon's owl). Draw a few feathers in pencil, showing the shaft and the soft edges.
Learn "The Star-Spangled Banner", the first four lines. (History learns them in week 27.) Clap its rhythm: it's in three (one-two-three), not four.
American Flamingo. Audubon had to bend the flamingo's long neck down to fit it life-size on the page.
Horn Concerto No. 4, the last movement (Rondo). The horn sounds like a hunting horn galloping along.
Finish the bird painting: add darker colors and details with a small brush, then the branch and leaves.
Measures in three: write and clap measures that add up to 3 beats (a half and a quarter; three quarters).

intro.text: Term-end conversation (week 30)
1. Who painted The Birds of America? How big did he paint each bird?
2. Which bird is your favorite? Describe the painting without looking.
3. Listen to three clips (Eine kleine Nachtmusik, the "Twinkle" variations, the horn concerto): who wrote them?
4. What did Mozart do as a child that amazed people?
5. How many quarter notes make a whole note? How many eighth notes make a half? Then sing "Shenandoah".
Memory Work card: Mozart (1756–1791), child prodigy, more than 600 works · John James Audubon (1785–1851), The Birds of America, life-size

blocks.text: Ruby-throated Hummingbird. Tiny hummingbirds around a flowering vine. Then lay out all six plates and choose a favorite.
"Ave verum corpus" (1791). A short, quiet prayer for choir, written in Latin in the last year of Mozart's life. (The child is learning Latin; listen for words like verum, "true".)
Mount the bird painting for the portfolio, with its name lettered underneath, as on Audubon's plates.
Sing "Shenandoah", "The Star-Spangled Banner" (first four lines) and "O God, Our Help in Ages Past" for the family.
Traditional, sung by river men and sailors in the 1800s (public domain). The first verse.
Oh Shenandoah, I long to see you,
Away, you rolling river.
Oh Shenandoah, I long to see you,
Away, I'm bound away
'Cross the wide Missouri.
The Missouri is the river Lewis and Clark followed west (History Term 5).
Words by Francis Scott Key, 1814 (public domain). The first verse.
O say can you see, by the dawn's early light,
What so proudly we hailed at the twilight's last gleaming,
Whose broad stripes and bright stars through the perilous fight,
O'er the ramparts we watched, were so gallantly streaming?
And the rocket's red glare, the bombs bursting in air,
Gave proof through the night that our flag was still there;
O say does that star-spangled banner yet wave
O'er the land of the free and the home of the brave?
The fractions link is the term's quiet gift. A child who can see that two halves make a whole in Arithmetic and in music has met the quadrivium's big idea: that number runs through everything.
Bird-watching is free. A feeder by a window gives a week's drawing models.
Two extinct birds. The Carolina parakeet and the passenger pigeon, both painted by Audubon, no longer exist. Children are often struck by this; it's a plain fact worth stating.

Watercolor paper and paints · brushes (one large, one small) · drawing pencils and sketchbook · a real feather · staff or plain paper for writing rhythms · printed or on-screen copies of the six plates · Mozart recordings

head: Composer
Ludwig van Beethoven (1770–1827): the bridge to Grade 4's Romantic composers
rows: Edward Hicks (1780–1849): American folk art, The Peaceable Kingdom
Stenciling, as folk artists decorated walls, floors and furniture
Folk-art patterns and borders · the year's portfolio gallery
"Oh! Susanna" (1848) · "Amazing Grace" (Bible's hymn) · the year's songs
Beethoven's famous rhythm · the "Ode to Joy" melody in solfège · review

reference.title: Where to find the paintings and music

blocks.text: Hicks's paintings are in the National Gallery of Art, the Philadelphia Museum of Art and other American museums. Free online images are easy to find, and all are in the public domain. Hicks painted The Peaceable Kingdom more than sixty times, so the versions differ; any will do.
Beethoven's music is among the most recorded in the world: free online, through a public library, or on any inexpensive recording.

Edward Hicks was born in Pennsylvania in 1780 and trained as a coach and sign painter. He was a Quaker minister, and painted in his spare time without formal training, which makes him a folk artist. His best-known pictures, The Peaceable Kingdom, show the prophecy in Isaiah 11 that the wolf and the lamb will live together, and often William Penn making his treaty in the background. (Bible read Isaiah in Term 4; History read about Penn in Term 2.)

Ludwig van Beethoven was born in Bonn, Germany, in 1770, and moved to Vienna as a young man to study with Haydn (Term 4). As he grew older he slowly went deaf, but he kept composing, hearing the music in his head. At the first performance of his Ninth Symphony in 1824 he could not hear the applause, and a singer turned him around to see the audience cheering. His music opens the Romantic era that Grade 4 studies.
The Peaceable Kingdom (one version, about 1834). Animals and children together; in the distance, William Penn and the Lenape.
Symphony No. 5, first movement. It begins with four notes: short-short-short-LONG. Listen for how many times they come back.

Design a stencil. Draw a simple shape (a heart, a star, a leaf, a tulip) on stiff card or a manila folder; the parent cuts it out with a craft knife. Folk artists used shapes like these over and over.
Learn "Oh! Susanna", the first verse and chorus. Beethoven's rhythm: clap short-short-short-LONG in different places in a song.
Penn's Treaty with the Indians. Hicks painted William Penn's treaty of 1682 many times. (History Term 2.)
"Für Elise", a short piano piece. Many piano students learn its opening.
Stencil on paper. Hold the stencil flat, dab paint through it with a sponge (not too wet), and lift it straight up. Practice until the edges come out clean.
Review the scale, do to high do, with hand signs. Sing "Oh! Susanna".
Noah's Ark (1846). The animals walking two by two toward the ark. (Bible Term 1.)

Symphony No. 6, "Pastoral", fourth movement, the thunderstorm, then the fifth, the shepherds' song of thanks. Compare it with Vivaldi's summer storm from Term 1: two composers, a hundred years apart, painting a storm in music.
A repeating border. Stencil the same shape again and again along the edge of a sheet, evenly spaced, like a folk-art wall border.
Listen to both storms again. Which is faster? Louder? Which do you like better, and why?
The Residence of David Twining, 1787 (painted 1840s). Hicks painted the farm where he grew up, as he remembered it as a boy.
Piano Sonata No. 14, "Moonlight", first movement. Quiet and slow. Someone later said it sounded like moonlight on a lake, and the name stuck.
Stencil something useful: a small wooden box, a board, a tote bag or a pillowcase (fabric paint), with the border or a single motif. (The Workshop track can supply a small box or board.)
"Ode to Joy" in solfège: mi mi fa sol · sol fa mi re · do do re mi · mi re re. Sing it slowly with hand signs.
The Cornell Farm (1848). A Pennsylvania farm with prize animals lined up in front, painted the year before Hicks died.
Symphony No. 9, the last movement: the "Ode to Joy". The tune the child sang in solfège last week, now sung by a huge choir. (The hymn "Joyful, Joyful, We Adore Thee" uses the same tune.)
Finish the stenciled piece and let it dry.
Sing "Ode to Joy" to la or in solfège, and "Amazing Grace".

weeks.title: The year's gallery and term-end conversation

intro.text: Term-end conversation (week 36)
1. Who painted The Peaceable Kingdom? What Bible prophecy does it show?
2. Why is Hicks called a folk artist?
3. Listen to the opening of the Fifth Symphony: who wrote it? What happened to his hearing?
4. Name the year's six composers in order, from Vivaldi to Beethoven.
5. Name the year's six artists, and one painting by each.
Memory Work card: Beethoven (1770–1827), composed even when deaf · Edward Hicks (1780–1849), folk artist, The Peaceable Kingdom

blocks.text: Another Peaceable Kingdom, a later version. Compare it with week 31's: what changed? Then lay out one favorite painting from each of the year's six artists and put them in order by date.
Name that composer. Play short clips of a favorite piece by each of the year's six composers, from Vivaldi to Beethoven. Can the child name each one?

Mount a small gallery of the year's work: a watercolor (Term 1), the sampler (Term 2), a silhouette (Term 3), a portrait (Term 4), the bird (Term 5) and the stencil (Term 6). Show it at Year-End Recitation Day (Memory Work, week 36).
Sing the year's songs: "Over the River", "Simple Gifts", "Yankee Doodle", "Chester", "My Country, 'Tis of Thee", "Shenandoah", "The Star-Spangled Banner", "Oh! Susanna".

blocks.text: For Grade 4: the Modern year's Romantic and modern composers begin where Beethoven leaves off.
Words and music by Stephen Foster, 1848 (public domain). The first verse and chorus.
I come from Alabama with my banjo on my knee,
I'm going to Louisiana, my true love for to see.
Oh! Susanna, oh don't you cry for me,
For I come from Alabama with my banjo on my knee.
The California gold miners of 1849 sang their own version: "I'm off to California with my washbowl on my knee." (History Term 6.)
Folk art is for everyone. Hicks had no formal training, and that's the point. Let the child's stencils be bold and simple.
Stencils need dry sponges. Too much paint bleeds under the edges. Dab, don't brush.
The year's gallery is a fine thing to show at Year-End Recitation Day alongside the recitations. Children are proud of a year's work laid out together.
